title: Should You Score Feedback Themes by Volume or by Rating?
summary: Volume and rating rank your feedback themes differently. When to use each, why an impact-ranked list can hide your biggest theme, and how to read both.
body_markdown:
Every theme list is sorted by something, and the sort decides what gets fixed. Rank by how many people mentioned a theme and you get the topics customers talk about most. Rank by how they rated it and you get the topics dragging your score down. The two lists rarely match, and teams argue about which one is real.


They measure different things, so the right one depends on the question you're asking. Thematic supports both. Its impact score tells you how much a theme moved your overall score, already adjusting for how many people mentioned it. Its volume score, available on lenses only, measures a theme by how many responses it drives rather than by how people rated it. Use rating-based impact when you have a score to attribute against and you're deciding what to fix to move it. Use volume when every response is an event that cost something, or when there's no meaningful rating to attribute against.


Below is what each score actually measures, the case where an impact-ranked list hides your biggest theme, and how to read the two together.


## What each score actually measures


Three numbers sit on a Thematic theme. They look similar and answer different questions.


- **Volume** , in the Themes Tool, is "the percentage of meaningful responses that mentioned each of the themes." It's a share of the conversation.
- **Score** is "the average score of each theme," meaning the average rating given by the people who mentioned it.
- **[Impact](https://help.getthematic.com/article/96-thematic-impact)** tells you "how much that theme increased or decreased your overall score," and it "takes into account the theme's volume as well as its score."


That last point is the one most teams miss. Impact is not the opposite of volume. Impact already contains volume. It weighs how badly a theme scores against how many people raised it, so a theme that scores terribly but was mentioned twice gets scaled down. That adjustment is what makes impact the right default when you're chasing a score.


One naming trap worth flagging. Volume in the Themes Tool is a percentage. A volume score, the capability described below, is a raw count. Same word, two different quantities.


## Why a theme can top the volume list and vanish from the impact list


Impact works by comparing a theme's responses against the overall average. Thematic defines it as "how much your overall score would have changed if you were to remove all comments mentioning that theme." So the size of a theme's impact depends on how far its raters sit from the mean.


Which means a theme whose raters sit *at* the mean produces almost no impact, however many people mention it. Remove it and the average barely moves. It can be the single most-discussed thing in your dataset and still sit near zero on an impact-ranked list.


That isn't a flaw in impact. It's impact working correctly, answering the question it was built for. It's still a blind spot when what you need to know is how much of something there is. Delivery timing, account access, billing queries: these get mentioned constantly by people who then rate you about average, because the issue was annoying rather than relationship-ending. An impact ranking tells you, accurately, that fixing them won't[move your net promoter score (NPS)](https://getthematic.com/insights/find-what-is-driving-nps-score) much. It won't tell you they're a fifth of your contact center volume.


Research on prioritization says the same thing from two directions. Nielsen Norman Group's[guidance on rating usability problems](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/how-to-rate-the-severity-of-usability-problems/) treats frequency as only one of three inputs, alongside "the impact of the problem if it occurs" and "the persistence of the problem," because no one of them ranks correctly alone. NN/g's Tanner Kohler makes the[inverse point about counting](https://www.nngroup.com/videos/frequency-in-qualitative-data/) : "Sometimes, the most valuable insights are mentioned only once."


## When to use each score


Use this When Because


Rating-based impact You have a score like NPS or CSAT attached to the feedback, and you're deciding what to fix to move it It weighs how badly a theme scores against how many people raised it


Volume as a score Every response is an event that had to be handled: a complaint, a call, a ticket The count is the thing you're trying to reduce, and it maps directly to workload


Volume as a score There's no meaningful rating attached, as with support queues, chat logs or open-ended research Impact needs a score to attribute against, and a volume score "doesn't need a score column"


Both, side by side You're setting a roadmap or a quarterly plan The[disagreements between the two lists](https://getthematic.com/insights/ai-powered-customer-feedback-theme-discovery) are the interesting part


One scope note, because Thematic's existing guidance is firmly[impact-first](https://getthematic.com/insights/extract-actionable-insights-customer-feedback) . Rank by impact rather than mention count wherever you have a score to attribute against. That guidance is about not letting raw frequency set the agenda when a better-adjusted number is available. It isn't a claim that counting is never the right measure. On a complaints inbox there's no score to adjust against, and the count is the point.


## How Thematic scores themes by volume


**Availability.**[Volume as a score](https://help.getthematic.com/article/231-volume-as-a-score) is available on lenses only. It isn't a setting you can turn on for any dataset.


**What it measures.** A volume score "measures a theme by how many responses it drives, not by how people rated it." The value is the raw count: "300 responses is a score of 300. It's a total, not an average and not a rate."


**Why a total.** Thematic's reasoning is operational. "Some datasets are made of events that cost something. In a complaints inbox, a contact centre or a support queue, every response is a real thing that happened and had to be handled." On that kind of data, "if account problems make up a fifth of your calls, halving them takes about a tenth of your calls away." An average can't be read that way, because it "tells you how bad something was, not how much of it there was."


**Where it shows up.** You select it from the[Score dropdown](https://getthematic.com/insights/link-feedback-themes-nps-csat-drivers) in the filter row. The Score Change view becomes a waterfall where "each bar is a number of responses," and written summaries "count in responses rather than points."


**How it's set up.** A lens admin configures it at Manage Lenses, then Configure Lens, then Scores, selecting Volume under Score Range and ticking which datasets to count.


**Across a lens, it adds.** "Two sources with 120 and 80 responses give a lens score of 200, not an average of 100."


## What this looks like when you're choosing what to fix


An online marketplace for home, consumer and insurance lending processes over 20,000 customer comments every 90 days. Its insights team found a "Timing of Call" theme disproportionately driving detractors in NPS surveys, then quantified the affected loan value to build a revenue case for fixing it. That's the rating-based path working exactly as intended: a theme that wasn't the loudest, but was the most expensive, surfaced because the score pointed at it.


A retailer with 84 stores and a three-person insights team analyzes roughly 20,000 verbatim comments a month. Its difficulty was "prioritising when 'everything seemed important'," and what changed was being able to see "exactly which topics had the biggest impact on our NPS scores" instead of "trying to tackle everything at once."


Both teams needed a ranking they could defend, and neither was served by a bare list of what came up most. The point isn't that volume beats rating or the reverse. A team with a score to chase should chase the score. A team drowning in handled events should count the events.


## What to check before you trust a volume score


- **Compare equal periods.** The score is a total, so it grows with the window. "A quarter has more responses in it than a month, so the score is larger but nothing has got worse."
- **Expect weighting to do nothing.** "If you turn weighting on, a volume score doesn't move," because inflating 300 calls to 450 "would report calls that never happened." Everything else on the page still weights normally.
- **Read waterfall bars as shares, not counts.** A response can carry several themes and some carry none, so a bar is "a theme's share of the change, not its own count." The theme list beside it shows the actual counts.
- **Remember it counts comments, not rows.** If a survey asks two open questions and someone answers both, that response contributes two.
- **Check whether your sample moved.** A volume shift can mean[your response base changed](https://getthematic.com/insights/quantify-themes-moved-nps-score) rather than your product. That caveat applies to any count, and it's the same reason a raw mention tally can over-weight[whoever answers most readily](https://getthematic.com/insights/feedback-representative-not-loudest-customers) .


## The short answer


Score by rating-based impact when you have a metric to attribute against and you're deciding what to fix to move it, because impact already weighs how badly a theme scores against how many people raised it. Score by volume when every response is an event that cost something to handle, or when there's no rating to attribute against. In Thematic, impact is available wherever your data has scores, and a volume score is available on lenses only. The useful test: pull both lists and look at what ranks high on one and nowhere on the other. That gap is usually the thing nobody is arguing about yet.
